concepts.name: Punch-Marked Coins (PMCs): Origins, Materials, and Historical Significance
key_dimensions: Earliest indigenous coinage of India (6th–2nd century BCE) predating Mauryan empire
Silver and copper as primary metals; absence of gold in early PMCs as a UPSC trap
Symbols on PMCs (sun, elephant, hill, tree) vs. absence of ruler's name/portrait — contrast with later coinage
PMCs as evidence for Mahajanapada-era trade networks and monetization of economy

concepts.name: Indo-Greek Coins: Bilingual and Bimetallic Innovations
key_dimensions: First coins in India to bear portrait of the issuing ruler — significance for political legitimacy
Bilingual (Greek + Kharosthi/Brahmi) and biscript character as evidence of cultural syncretism
Introduction of gold coinage tradition into northwestern India
Menander I (Milinda) coins as overlap between numismatics, Buddhism (Milindapanha), and political history

concepts.name: Kushana Gold Coinage (Dinara): Economy and Religious Syncretism
key_dimensions: Kanishka's coins depicting Buddha, Shiva, Mithra, Nana — evidence of Kushana religious eclecticism
High gold purity as indicator of prosperous trans-continental Silk Route trade
Term 'Dinara' borrowed from Roman 'Denarius' — evidence of Roman economic influence
Kushana coins as primary source for reconstructing the dynastic sequence and ruler portraits

concepts.name: Gupta Gold Coins (Dinaras): Typology and Cultural Interpretation
key_dimensions: Multiple coin types (Archer, Lyrist, Tiger-slayer, Ashvamedha) as evidence for Gupta king's persona and imperial ideology
Samudragupta's coins as corroboration for Allahabad Pillar inscription — cross-source validation
Decline in gold purity in later Gupta coins as numismatic evidence for economic decline
Chandragupta II's coins depicting him as 'Vikramaditya' — coins as propaganda tools

concepts.name: Satavahana Lead and Potin Coins: Regional Economy and Trade
key_dimensions: Predominance of lead coins (unique to Satavahanas) as evidence for local/regional rather than long-distance trade
Bilingual coins (Prakrit + Tamil/Telugu) as evidence for Deccan cultural interface
Ship motif on coins as direct numismatic evidence for maritime trade in the Deccan
Gautamiputra Satakarni's coins as corroboration for Nasik Prasasti — cross-referencing trap

concepts.name: Roman Coins in India: Evidence for Indo-Roman Trade
key_dimensions: Concentration of finds at Coimbatore, Karur, Arikamedu, Kolhapur — mapping trade routes
Defacement/countermarking of Roman coins as evidence that they were used as bullion, not currency
Augustus and Tiberius coins dominating finds — chronological evidence for peak of Indo-Roman trade (1st century CE)
Pliny's complaint about gold drain to India as literary corroboration for numismatic evidence

concepts.name: Coins as Evidence for Dynastic Chronology and Succession
key_dimensions: Indo-Greek dynastic sequence reconstructed almost entirely from coins (literary sources are sparse)
Overlapping coin finds used to establish co-regencies (e.g., Kushana rulers)
Coin hoards indicating terminus post quem and terminus ante quem for dating events
Blank periods in coin evidence vs. dark ages — methodological limitation

concepts.name: Coin Legends and Scripts as Linguistic-Historical Source
key_dimensions: Kharosthi (right-to-left) on Indo-Greek/Indo-Scythian coins vs. Brahmi on Satavahana/Gupta coins
Greek, Prakrit, Sanskrit, Tamil legends indicating the administrative language of the issuing authority
Transition from Prakrit to Sanskrit in coin legends as marker of Brahmanical resurgence (post-Kushana)
Earliest use of Sanskrit in official records traced partly through coin legends

concepts.name: Iconography on Coins as Evidence for Religious History
key_dimensions: Earliest numismatic depiction of Buddha in human form on Kushana coins (contrast with aniconic tradition)
Lakshmi, Garuda, and Vishnu on Gupta coins as evidence for Vaishnava resurgence
Shiva and bull (Nandi) iconography on Kushana coins predating Shaiva Puranic tradition
Coin iconography as cross-reference with sculptural and textual sources — overlap/trap area

concepts.name: Coin Hoards: Methodology and Historical Interpretation
key_dimensions: Hoard composition (mixed vs. uniform) as indicator of savings vs. commercial transactions
Increased hoard finds in a region as evidence for political instability or invasion
Bayana Hoard (Gupta gold coins) — largest Gupta hoard, significance for art and economic history
Methodological trap: absence of hoards ≠ absence of coins; burial practices and survival bias

concepts.name: Debasement of Coinage as Economic Indicator
key_dimensions: Late Gupta silver coinage debasement as numismatic evidence for fiscal stress and Huna invasions
Comparison: Roman debasement under crisis vs. Indian patterns — UPSC comparative angle
Debasement vs. change in denomination — distinguishing the two as a conceptual trap
Karshapana weight standard variations as evidence for economic regionalization

concepts.name: Weight Standards and Metrology in Ancient Indian Coins
key_dimensions: Karshapana (3.3 grams approx.) as standard for PMCs — Arthashastra reference as corroboration
Suvarna/Nishka as gold weight units — overlap between Vedic literature and numismatic evidence
Variability in PMC weights across regions as evidence for absence of centralized monetary authority
Ratti (0.11 grams) as base unit — continuity from ancient to medieval period

concepts.name: Tribal and Janapada Coins: Evidence for Pre-Mauryan Political Economy
key_dimensions: Coins issued by Yaudheyas, Malavas, Kunindas as evidence for post-Mauryan republican/oligarchic polities
Tribal coins bearing collective names (not individual rulers) vs. monarchical coins — political contrast
Geographic distribution of Janapada coins mapping political boundaries
These coins as primary (sometimes only) evidence for tribes mentioned in Mahabharata/Puranas — overlap trap

concepts.name: Western Kshatrapa (Shaka) Coins: Chronology and Regional History
key_dimensions: Unique regnal year system on Shaka coins enabling precise dating — methodological importance
Bilingual (Greek + Brahmi) transitioning to purely Brahmi — evidence for Indianization of Shakas
Rudradaman's coins as corroboration for Junagadh Rock Inscription
Contrast with Kushana dating system — trap on which dynasty used which chronological marker on coins

concepts.name: Limitations of Numismatics as a Historical Source
key_dimensions: Coins represent elite/state economy — silent on village/barter economy (methodological gap)
Forgeries and imitations (e.g., Kushana imitations by Kidarites) complicate interpretation
Findspot reliability: coins travel far from origin — cannot always indicate local economy
Absence of coins for certain dynasties (e.g., Kanva, some Satavahana rulers) creates historical blind spots

concepts.name: Sangam-Era Tamil Coins and Trade Tokens
key_dimensions: Tamil coins bearing fish (Pandya), tiger (Chola), bow (Chera) as dynastic symbols — corroboration with Sangam literature
Lead and copper dominance in south Indian coins vs. gold/silver in north — economic differentiation
Integration of Roman coin evidence with indigenous Tamil coin finds for trade route mapping
Coins as corroboration for Sangam poems mentioning markets (angadi) and merchants (vaniga)

concepts.name: Arthashastra's Numismatic References: Text-Coin Cross Validation
key_dimensions: Arthashastra mentions Lakshadhyaksha (superintendent of mint) — numismatic evidence for state-controlled coinage
Prescribed alloy compositions in Arthashastra vs. actual coin metallurgy as test of state control
Arthashastra's mention of 'Rupyadarshaka' (coin examiner) as evidence for sophisticated monetary administration
Discrepancies between Arthashastra prescriptions and actual Mauryan PMC evidence — a UPSC trap area

concepts.name: Numismatics and Gender History: Queens and Women on Ancient Coins
key_dimensions: Prabhavati Gupta's coins as evidence for female regency in Gupta period
Naganika (Satavahana queen) — rare female ruler evidenced partly through inscriptions, coins absent — trap
Depictions of goddesses (Lakshmi, Sri) on coins vs. actual ruling queens — distinguishing religious iconography from political evidence
Comparative absence of women rulers on coins vs. inscriptional evidence — methodological cross-check

concepts.name: Coin Evidence for Trade Guilds (Shrenis) and Merchant Corporations
key_dimensions: Guild-issued coins (e.g., Kushana-era guild tokens) as evidence for private/semi-private monetary activity
Merchant symbols on PMCs potentially linked to guild marks — debated interpretation
Coins as evidence for the role of Shresthins and Sarthavahas in monetized economy
Cross-reference with epigraphic evidence (Nasik, Sanchi inscriptions) mentioning guild endowments
